title: The Sun’s magnetic poles swap places about every 11 years

cover.alt: The Sun in golden ultraviolet light, its disc mottled with a few bright patches, seen by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory in 2010.
cover.credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/SDO · Public domain

body: The Sun’s activity rises and falls on a cycle that lasts **about 11 years** on average. At its peak, the solar maximum, the Sun is covered in sunspots and bright, tangled regions and fires off far more flares; at the minimum it goes almost quiet. The cycle is magnetic: the moving, spinning plasma inside the Sun winds up its magnetic field, and around each maximum the Sun’s overall field flips, so its north and south magnetic poles trade places. It takes two cycles, about 22 years, for the field to return to how it started.

slides.alt: Time-lapse of the Sun in golden ultraviolet light: its disc fills with bright, tangled active regions, which then fade until the Sun is an almost featureless glow.
slides.caption: Ten years of the Sun seen by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory from 2010, sped up 2×: activity swells to a peak around 2014, then dies down towards the quiet minimum of late 2019.
slides.credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/SDO · Public domain · excerpt, sped up 2×, blank frames cut

slides.label: for the Sun’s magnetic field to flip and flip back again
slides.text: The field reverses near each solar maximum, so it takes two 11-year cycles, together called a Hale cycle, to return to its starting state.

slides.heading: Flares of a given size, solar minimum vs maximum
slides.note: Flares of any given size are some 50 times more frequent at solar maximum

slides.prompt: The cycle averages 11 years, but it isn’t a perfect clock. What range of lengths have astronomers seen?
slides.detail: Cycle 24, the one in the clip, began in January 2008 and ended in December 2019, after 11.0 years.

slides.question: How did Samuel Schwabe discover the solar cycle in 1843?
slides.explanation: Schwabe noticed a regular rise and fall in the average number of sunspots after 17 years of watching the Sun, and kept observing until 1867.
